summary: Round 2. No code and no tests in this diff -- four files, ~50 lines, all prose -- so there is no production line to mutate and no test to weigh. Reviewed, as in round 1, as the falsifiability of the criteria M5.45f/g/h will be built and tested against. ALL THREE ROUND-1 MAJORS ARE CLOSED WITH REAL WORDING, NOT A RESTATEMENT OF THE DEFECT. (a) M5.45h criterion 1 now reads 'issues ONE fetch AND ALL K RUNS DECODE THEIR OWN RECORDS FROM IT', which kills the coalescing-by-empty-array mutation exactly (first delivery fetches, other 63 get new byte[0]: fetch count still 1, residency bound still intact, failure sentence still true, 63 shards ingest nothing) -- that implementation now fails a numbered criterion. (b) The same criterion now says the fake counts INVOCATIONS, not distinct urls, and gives the reason in the row rather than leaving it in DirectServingTest's javadoc: a Set<String> of requested urls reads 1 under the per-run implementation too, because all K deliveries carry the same key-scoped Grant and Grant has value equality. (c) M5.45g gains criterion 4 (bytes DECODED through ConsumerClient, test fetcher serves only the exact url in the ARRIVING grant and throws otherwise, observed url asserted equal to the minted one) -- that kills BOTH surviving mutations I measured: a no-op DIRECT path yielding zero records, and a ConsumerClient that builds its own Grant or ignores the one on the Delivery, which a bytes-decoded assertion alone would not have caught against a deterministic single-segment fetcher. Criterion 6 keeps the un-coalesced production fetcher from shipping and makes the flag default ASSERTED, which is a falsifiable form. Both round-1 minors are addressed too: M5.45f criterion 3 now names the five grep patterns and demands a per-site disposition list, and the two stale ADR-0043 pointers at :77 and :105 that the finding cited are corrected in this diff, along with the present-tense Cost paragraph that M5.45d had falsified. I also re-walked old M5.45c's five criteria against the three successors for a dropped obligation, which is what the M5.45b split lost: (1)->g1, (2)->g2, (3)->g3 (strengthened with ADR-0023's dependency check), (4)->f1, (5)->h1/h2 plus the coordinates question at f(b); the range parameter is the one thing deliberately not carried, and the reason and its owner are recorded in both the row and ADR-0043's Status. Nothing dropped, nothing weakened. THREE MINORS REMAIN, ALL THE SAME SHAPE AND NONE BLOCKING: three criteria across the two future rows are satisfied by a SENTENCE rather than by a case, so the behaviour they name ships unpinned. They are recorded rather than fixed (review.md rule 11) -- each is a one-word change the taker of that row can make, and the row's own review is where a missing case is visible.

findings.title: M5.45g criterion 5 demands that a failing fetch 'HAS STATED BEHAVIOUR' -- a javadoc sentence satisfies it, so the behaviour it names ships with no case
findings.failure_scenario: The round-1 finding was that no row said what a failing direct fetch does. The new criterion 5 answers it in the register of documentation: 'A FETCH THAT FAILS HAS STATED BEHAVIOUR -- an expired grant, a 403, a truncated body'. Criteria 3 and 4 beside it carry assertion verbs ('ASSERTED rather than assumed', 'the assertion is on bytes DECODED'); criterion 5 carries none. SURVIVING IMPLEMENTATION: the seam's javadoc states 'a fetcher that throws propagates out of readNext and the offset does not advance', and ConsumerClient.decodeInto wraps the fetch in try/catch returning an empty record list with the offset advanced -- no case exists either way. Criterion 5 is green on the sentence, criteria 1-4 and 6 are untouched, and the exact silent data loss the criterion was written to forbid is what ships. This is narrower than the round-1 finding it fixes (the forbidden outcome is now named in the row, so an author who reads it cannot claim the swallow was intended), which is why it is minor rather than the major it would have been in round 1.
findings.suggestion: One word: 'A FETCH THAT FAILS HAS STATED BEHAVIOUR, ASSERTED -- a case in which the fetcher throws and readNext fails that run visibly rather than yielding an empty batch'.

findings.title: M5.45h criteria 2 and 3 are 'NAMED AND BUDGETED' and 'are stated' -- the per-node hold can leak and the all-or-none rule can be false while all three criteria read green
findings.failure_scenario: Criterion 1 was fixed and is now falsifiable; its two neighbours were not touched and neither demands a case. SURVIVING IMPLEMENTATION for criterion 2: the node-scoped owner holds fetched segments in a Map<SegmentKey, byte[]> and never evicts. The K=64 case in criterion 1 uses ONE segment, so the invocation count is still 1 and all 64 runs decode their own records; criterion 2 is satisfied by a javadoc naming C = 8 MiB, which is simply false after the second segment; criterion 3 is untouched. The row itself concedes the only gate that could see it cannot: 'a hold of C is flat in K at every K, so criterion 6 cannot tell C = 8 MiB from C = 8 GiB'. Result is unbounded heap growth inside the OpenSearch node process. The row's own analogy points at the fix -- M5.40b's SegmentCache ships theCEILINGHoldsHoweverManySegmentsArePut and aSegmentLARGERThanTheCeilingIsREFUSED (ingest/src/test/java/binjava/ingest/SegmentCacheTest.java:44,72) -- so the precedent is asserted and the criterion that cites it is not. SURVIVING IMPLEMENTATION for criterion 3: on a failed fetch the owner logs once and completes all 64 per-key queues with empty batches; 'one failed fetch fails every run that node holds' is stated in prose, every run did see the same outcome, and no case distinguishes 'fails' from 'is quietly emptied'. Minor and not major because both clauses predate this diff unchanged -- I did not raise them in round 1 -- and because escalating a pre-existing criterion at round 2 would trigger rule 12's split remedy on a 50-line prose commit, which is not what rule 12 is for.
findings.suggestion: Add the assertion to each: criterion 2 'the bound is asserted -- a case shows the hold released after the last of the K runs decodes, or a ceiling of N segments refusing the N+1th, as SegmentCacheTest does'; criterion 3 'asserted: a failing fetch fails all K runs visibly rather than completing them with empty batches'.

findings.title: M5.45f criterion 3's artifact lands in the commit body, which neither reviewer is shown and no gate diffs
findings.failure_scenario: The fix is good in its checkable half: naming byteStart, byteLen, M5.44, ADR-0043 and VERSION_3 makes the sweep re-runnable by anyone, which is what round 1 asked for. The artifact's placement is the residual. scripts/review.sh emits no commit message into either packet (no git log, no COMMIT_EDITMSG), so the site list is invisible to the reviewer and the test-reviewer at the moment they judge whether the sweep happened, and it is outside the diff hash that binds their verdicts. SURVIVING RUN: the taker of M5.45f greps, finds six sites, lists five with dispositions in the commit body and misses one -- say a javadoc still claiming the coordinates are read by a consumer. check-links and check-adr-refs pass (the reference resolves, it is merely false), both reviewers see a diff with no list in it, the commit lands, and the omission is only discoverable by someone re-running the grep later. Rung 4 of the gate-design ladder is one step away: the same list in ADR-0043 is diffable against the tree.
findings.suggestion: Put the site list in ADR-0043 next to decision (b), or in the row's own state cell, rather than only in the commit body -- then a missed site is a difference between committed text and a grep, and it is inside the bytes the next review is bound to.
